clinicalPearls: A heterogeneous group of inherited disorders defined by ineffective erythropoiesis and pathognomonic multinuclearity and dysplastic changes of bone marrow erythroblasts, with an anaemia that is characteristically reticulocytopenic for its severity
Type II (SEC23B) is the commonest form; type I (CDAN1, more rarely CDIN1) and type III (KIF23) are rarer, and transcription-factor variants (e.g. GATA1, KLF1) are increasingly recognised
Presentation ranges from antenatal or neonatal anaemia and hydrops through to incidental diagnosis in adulthood; jaundice, splenomegaly and pigment gallstones are common

The anaemia is typically normocytic or macrocytic with an inappropriately low reticulocyte count, reflecting intramedullary destruction of abnormal erythroblasts rather than peripheral haemolysis alone
Parenchymal iron overload develops even without transfusion because ineffective erythropoiesis suppresses hepcidin, and it may be the dominant clinical problem

Type II red cells show increased lysis by acidified ABO-compatible sera (the historical acidified-serum, or Ham, reaction) reflecting abnormal membrane band 3 glycosylation, hence the older name HEMPAS

Marrow morphology guides typing (binucleate erythroblasts in type II, internuclear chromatin bridges and megaloblastoid change in type I, giant multinucleate erythroblasts in type III), now confirmed by molecular genetics
Careful distinction from myelodysplasia, thalassaemia and other causes of ineffective erythropoiesis is essential to avoid inappropriate therapy
reference.pathophysiology: The congenital dyserythropoietic anaemias arise from mutations in genes governing erythroblast nuclear division, cytokinesis and membrane maturation. Type I reflects defects in codanin-1 (CDAN1) or CDIN1 that disturb chromatin and nuclear architecture, type II results from SEC23B mutations impairing COPII-mediated vesicular transport and glycosylation of membrane proteins such as band 3, and type III arises from KIF23 mutations disrupting cytokinesis. The common consequence is apoptosis and destruction of morphologically abnormal erythroid precursors within the marrow, so effective red cell output fails to match demand. The resulting ineffective erythropoiesis, together with hepcidin suppression driven by erythroferrone and related mediators, produces anaemia and progressive parenchymal iron loading that is independent of transfusion.
additionalDifferentials: Myelodysplastic syndrome with ring sideroblasts or multilineage dysplasia
Thalassaemia syndromes and other causes of ineffective erythropoiesis
Megaloblastic anaemia from vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Hereditary haemolytic anaemias (membrane, enzyme or unstable haemoglobin defects)
Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, given the historical acidified-serum overlap
Hereditary haemochromatosis, when the iron-loading phenotype dominates
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with red cell indices and reticulocyte count (characteristically low for the anaemia)
Blood film for anisopoikilocytosis and basophilic stippling
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine for characteristic erythroblast morphology and to exclude myelodysplasia
Bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin as markers of haemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis
Iron studies with ferritin and transferrin saturation, plus hepatic and cardiac MRI (T2*) for iron quantification
Targeted gene sequencing or a CDA panel (SEC23B, CDAN1, CDIN1, KIF23, GATA1, KLF1)
Exclusion tests including haemoglobin analysis and flow cytometry for a paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria clone
redFlags: Antenatal presentation with hydrops fetalis or severe neonatal anaemia
Iron overload with cardiac, hepatic or endocrine dysfunction
Symptomatic pigment gallstones or biliary obstruction
Aplastic crisis, for example with parvovirus B19, causing abrupt worsening
reference.prognosis: Many patients follow a mild to moderate course compatible with a normal lifespan, but morbidity is driven chiefly by iron overload and its complications. Transfusion-dependent forms and those with unrecognised iron loading fare less well, although much of this is preventable with monitoring and chelation.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing CDA as myelodysplasia and exposing young patients to inappropriate therapy
Overlooking iron overload because the patient has never been transfused
Attributing an inappropriately low reticulocyte count to marrow failure rather than ineffective erythropoiesis
Missing the diagnosis in a mildly anaemic adult labelled as chronic haemolysis of unknown cause
Assuming splenectomy is curative, when it may reduce transfusion needs but does not correct ineffective erythropoiesis and carries thrombotic and infective risk
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Treat parenchymal iron overload with iron chelation therapy, monitored by ferritin, transferrin saturation and hepatic and cardiac MRI T2*, as loading occurs even without transfusion
Provide judicious red cell transfusion for symptomatic or transfusion-dependent anaemia
Give interferon-alpha for type I (CDAN1) disease, which frequently responds
Supplement folic acid to meet erythropoietic demand
Consider splenectomy in selected cases to improve haemoglobin, with pneumococcal and other vaccination and thromboprophylaxis
Surveil for pigment gallstones and perform cholecystectomy when symptomatic
Undertake molecular subclassification (SEC23B, CDAN1, CDIN1, KIF23) with genetic counselling, and consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for severe disease through a haematology service
